previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: An elderly male with a history of COPD, alcohol dependence, dementia, and chronic aspiration was admitted for acute respiratory failure and septic shock due to aspiration pneumonia. He required ICU care, vasopressor support, and broad-spectrum antibiotics. A central line was placed initially, later replaced with a PICC line. He was treated for concurrent COPD exacerbation and mild heart failure with steroids and diuretics. Hyponatremia was managed with fluid restriction. Goals of care were discussed, confirming the patient's DNR/DNI status and refusal of a feeding tube despite high aspiration risk. He improved clinically, was stabilized on oxygen, and transitioned to extended care with plans to complete IV antibiotics and outpatient follow-up for pulmonary and swallowing issues.
problems: Pneumonitis due to inhalation of food and vomit
Syndrome of inappropriate secretion of antidiuretic hormone
Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with (acute) exacerbation

Discharge Instructions:
Dear Mr. ___, 

You were admitted to the hospital because you white blood cell 
count (marker of inflammation or infection) was increasing.  We 
felt that this was likely due to some food going into your lungs 
(aspiration) as was discussed when you were in the hospital last 
time.  We looked for other types of infection and did not find 
any indication of any other infections.  Your elevated white 
blood cells (inflammatory cells) is likely from irritation on 
the lungs from your aspiration and not from infection.

If you develop any signs or symptoms of infection such as fever, 
cough, sputum production, or any other symptoms that concern 
you, please return to the hospital.  Finally, you and your 
family understand the risks for ongoing aspiration as was 
discussed during your last hospitalization.  You all have 
elected to continue eating despite understanding these risks.

It was a pleasure taking care of you, 

-Your ___ Team
